cues: Welcome to Claude Automations — the complete visual guide.
Prepared by Sara Salem.
In this video, you'll learn how Claude can work for you automatically — on a schedule, or when something happens — and how to build your own automations, step by step.
Let's start with a simple comparison.
Doing work manually means you remember to start it, you copy information between apps, and you repeat the same steps every day or every week. It's easy to forget, and it takes time.

With an automation, Claude does the work for you. It starts at the right moment, gathers the information, follows your instructions, and delivers the result — even while you're busy with something else.
You stay in control, and you get your time back.
So, what exactly is a Claude automation?
It's a task that Claude runs automatically, built from four simple parts.
A trigger decides when it runs — for example, every weekday at 8 a.m.
Instructions tell Claude what to do, in plain language.
Connectors give Claude access to your tools, like email, calendar, or Slack. And the output is the result Claude delivers — a summary, a report, a file, or a message.
Let's follow one automation from start to finish.
First, the trigger fires — the schedule is reached, or an event happens.
Claude reads the saved instructions for this automation.
Then it uses its tools and connectors to gather information and do the work.
It produces the output, in the format you asked for.
And finally, it delivers the result — to your inbox, a Slack channel, a document, or a code repository.
Where can Claude automations run? There are several options, from no code at all to fully custom.
Scheduled tasks in the Claude desktop app let anyone run a prompt automatically, on a schedule — no code needed.
Routines in Claude Code on the web run a saved prompt on a schedule, with each run starting in a fresh cloud session.
Hooks in Claude Code run your own commands automatically, at key moments while Claude works.
GitHub Actions let Claude respond to events in your repository — like a new pull request, or a comment mentioning Claude.
Headless mode lets you run Claude Code from scripts and command-line jobs, without the interactive interface.
And the Claude API and Managed Agents let developers build automations right into their own products and systems.
Now, let's build an automation step by step. Step one: pick the right task.
The best candidates are tasks you repeat often — every day or every week — with clear steps that are the same each time.
This illustrative chart shows how much time a few common tasks can take each week, before and after automation.
Look for tasks where a small mistake is easy to catch and fix — like a draft summary you'll review — and start there.
Step two: choose the trigger. This decides when your automation runs.
A schedule runs it at fixed times — every morning, every Monday, or at the end of each month.
An event runs it when something happens — like a new pull request, or a file being edited.
On demand means you start it yourself, with a command or a button, whenever you need it.
And an API call lets your own systems start the automation, as part of a bigger process.
Step three: write clear instructions. This is the heart of your automation.
Start with the goal, and note the schedule — here, a morning briefing every weekday.
List the steps Claude should follow — reading the calendar, scanning recent emails, and flagging what's urgent.
Describe the output exactly — in this case, a short summary with three sections.
And say where to deliver it, plus any rules — like never sending emails on your behalf.
Step four: connect the tools your automation needs.
Connectors let Claude work with email, calendars, and team chat — like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Slack.
They also cover files, code, and notes — like Google Drive, GitHub, and Notion.
And business tools, like Linear and HubSpot. Connect only what the automation really needs — and remember that available connectors depend on your plan and your organization's settings.
Step five: choose where your automation will run.
If you don't write code, scheduled tasks in the Claude app are the simplest choice.
If your work lives in code repositories, Claude Code routines can run your prompt in the cloud on a schedule.
If you want Claude to react to repository events, use the GitHub Actions integration.
And if you're building automation into your own product, use the Claude API, or Managed Agents.
Step six: build it. Let's look at three examples, starting with GitHub Actions.
First, choose the event that triggers the workflow — here, a new comment on an issue or pull request.
Add a condition, so it only runs when someone mentions Claude.
Then use Anthropic's Claude Code action, which runs Claude on the repository.
And pass your API key securely, as a repository secret — never written directly in the file.
The second example is hooks, which automate actions inside Claude Code itself.
A hook listens for an event — here, post tool use, which fires right after Claude uses a tool.
The matcher picks which tools it applies to — whenever Claude edits or writes a file.
The command runs automatically — in this example, a formatter that tidies the code.
Now every file Claude touches is formatted consistently, without anyone having to remember.
The third example is headless mode, for scripts and scheduled jobs.
With the dash p flag, Claude runs a single task from the command line, and prints the result.
You can limit exactly which tools it's allowed to use, and ask for JSON output, so other programs can read it.
Then schedule it with a tool like cron — for example, every weekday at 8 a.m.
This turns any repeatable task into a reliable, automatic job.
Step seven: add guardrails. Automations run without you watching, so safety matters.
When the trigger fires, the automation starts with only the access you've given it.
Permissions control which tools and connectors it can use.
Limits — like the maximum number of turns, timeouts, and spending caps — keep it from running too long.
For sensitive actions, like sending messages or changing data, require a human to review and approve.
And keep logs of every run, so you can always see what happened, and why.
Step eight: test and monitor your automation.
Run it manually a few times first, and check every result carefully.
Then let it run on its schedule, and track how it performs over time — the success rate, failures, and time saved.
In this illustrative example, small improvements to the instructions raise the success rate week after week.
Review the logs regularly, and update the instructions whenever your needs change.
Here are six best practices for great Claude automations.
One: start small, with one simple task, and expand from there.
Two: write clear instructions, with an exact output format.
Three: give the minimum access needed — only the tools and data the task requires.
Four: keep a human in the loop for anything that sends, deletes, or changes things.
Five: test before you schedule, and watch the first few runs closely.
And six: review and improve regularly, so your automations stay useful.
Let's recap in one line: trigger, run, deliver.
Claude automations turn repetitive work into reliable routines — so you can focus on the work that matters most.
